source_document.body:
Containerized imports through U.S ports reached a record 2.67 million twenty foot equivalent units (TEUs) in October, pushing volumes above the previous peak set during the pandemic-era surge.
Rising shipments from China and a rebound at East and Gulf Coast ports fueled the record, according to Descartes data.
Imports totaled 2,674,808 TEUs, up 5% from September and 16% from October 2025. The total exceeded the previous monthly record of 2,622,465 TEUs, set in May 2022, by 2%.
The increase lifted imports for the first 10 months of 2026 to 2.3% above the same period a year earlier. October marked the second consecutive month in which cumulative imports ran ahead of 2025, following eight months below the prior year’s pace.
Imports from China rose for a fourth consecutive month, reaching 987,805 TEUs, and the highest monthly total since January 2025. Volumes increased 6.9% from September and 22.9% from a year earlier, accounting for approximately half of the overall U.S. monthly gain.
China’s share of U.S. container imports increased to 36.9%, from 36.3% in September. Plastics, furniture and bedding, and toys, games and sporting goods were the largest categories by volume.
Growth extended beyond China as imports from the top 10 countries of origin increased 5.8% from September, with seven posting gains. South Korea and Germany each recorded monthly increases of 22.8%, while Vietnam, Taiwan and India declined. All 10 origins recorded higher volumes than in October 2025.
East and Gulf Coast ports gain ground
Houston recorded the largest monthly volume increase among the top 10 U.S. ports, adding 42,665 TEUs, a gain of 26.7%. Savannah imports rose 12.6%, Norfolk increased 17.7%, and Charleston’s climbed 18.6%. By contrast, volumes fell 1.4% at Los Angeles, 2% at Long Beach and 10.9% at Oakland.
The gains shifted a larger share of imports toward East and Gulf Coast gateways. The five leading ports in those regions handled 39.9% of U.S. container imports, up from 36.7% in September. The five leading West Coast gateways’ share fell to 44.9%, from 47%.
Across the Gulf Coast, imports increased 24% to 266,905 TEUs, the highest monthly total since Descartes began tracking the regional measure in August 2023. Houston accounted for approximately 83% of the region’s net monthly increase.
Descartes cautioned that the sharp gains partly reflected a recovery from September’s weaker volumes. Combined imports at Houston, Savannah, Norfolk and Charleston rose 18.1% month over month but were only 3.6% above August levels. Extended peak-season demand and uneven vessel arrival timing may also have contributed, the report said.
Transit delays build alongside higher volumes
The record month followed a sustained period of elevated imports, with monthly volumes exceeding 2.5 million TEUs since July. Meanwhile, the unweighted average transit delay across 10 tracked gateways increased to 6.3 days in October, from six days in September and 4.2 days in June.
Seven of the 10 gateways recorded higher delays in October. Descartes said the gradual increase could indicate that sustained import volumes were putting pressure on the inland logistics network, although November’s data would help establish whether that pressure was intensifying.
The report’s transit-delay measure compares the estimated arrival date initially declared on a bill of lading with the date Descartes receives the corresponding U.S. Customs and Border Protection-processed data. The underlying import figures use an initial compilation of customs bill-of-lading records and may be revised.
Policy and routing risks remain
Beyond port performance, Descartes flagged changing maritime fees, canal availability and security conditions as planning risks. The Trump administration suspended port fees on Chinese ships through January 9, 2027, while increased Panama Canal transit availability and selected returns to Suez Canal routings were changing options on some services. Services through the Suez remained dependent on regional security conditions, the report noted.
Closer to home, the report indicated concerns over ongoing contract talks with watchmen at Los Angeles and Long Beach represented by the International Longshore and Warehouse Union , with the contract extended through November 20. Employers warned that a potential strike could affect terminals handling more than half of the two ports’ combined cargo.
Why it matters: October’s record shows import volumes reaching new highs despite year-to-date growth that remains modest, with resulting pressure distributed unevenly across ports.
